Literals and Constants

Stage 2 Concept ⏱ 12 min 📖 Glossary

Literals are values typed directly into code: 42, 3.5, single letters, quoted text, true. Constants (final) give important ones names, so magic numbers stop haunting the codebase.

🔎 Motivating questionWhy do buildings label doors “EXIT” instead of painting mysterious green rectangles everywhere?

Objectives

  • Spot literals in code
  • Use final constants
  • Apply L, f, and text rules

Needs first: Reference Types and Object References

1 Start with an analogy

Real life first, code second.

Name tags versus sticky notes. The number 3.14159 scribbled in twenty places is twenty sticky notes that rot separately. final double PI = 3.14159 is one engraved tag — a single truth, reused safely.

⚠️ Where the analogy breaksWhere it breaks: engraved tags cannot be re-engraved. final is a compiler-enforced promise — reassigning it breaks the build ON PURPOSE, loudly, at once.

2 The concept, plainly

One idea at a time, words before jargon.

Integer literals are int by birth (add L for long). Decimal literals are double (add f for float). Single quotes make char, double quotes make String, and 1_000_000 shows underscores are human-only decoration.

final double PI = 3.14159; names a constant: assigned exactly once, then locked. Convention writes constants in UPPER_CASE so they visually shout “do not touch”.

Char and escape details: ’\n’ is newline, ’\t’ is tab, ’\\’ is one backslash. Inside "..." the same escapes work, so "a\nb" prints two lines.

Java 17 also offers text blocks (“""...""”) for multi-line strings — HTML, SQL, JSON without plus-chains. Preview now, master later.

⚙️ Tech details — precise facts
  • Underscores may sit BETWEEN digits only: 1_000 ok, _100 and 100_ are illegal. Bases: 0b101 (binary), 017 (octal!), 0xFF (hex) — note the sneaky leading-zero octal.
  • final on a reference locks the SLIP, not the house: final StringBuilder sb can still append. Immutability and final-ness are different ideas.
  • A magic number is any unexplained literal in logic. Name it, and the code starts documenting itself.

3 Watch it move: Sticky notes become name tags

Step at your pace. Text explains every move.

4 Live code demo

Small, correct Java 17 (LTS) code. Read, trace, copy.

Main.javaJava 17
public class Main {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    final double PI = 3.14159; // engraved tag
    int count = 1000;
    long big = 5000000000L;
    double circle = PI * 2 * 2; // 2πr with r = 2
    System.out.println("PI = " + PI);
    System.out.println("count = " + count);
    System.out.println("circle = " + circle);
  }
}
▶ Output PI = 3.14159 count = 1000 circle = 12.56636
  • PI is named once, then reused — change it in one place.
  • The L suffix makes the huge literal a long.
  • circle computes 3.14159 × 4 = 12.56636.
▶️ Run it yourselfSave exactly as Main.java, then javac Main.java and java Main. Every full program in this course works this way.
💡 Why this output?Named constant keeps every use consistent; the math is plain 2πr with r = 2.

6 Common mistakes (at least 3)

Wrong, why, fixed — learn from realistic slips.

❌ Mistake 1: The same 0.18 tax rate scattered across 20 lines.Why: One law change means 20 edits — and you WILL miss one.
✅ Fix: final double TAX_RATE = 0.18; then reuse TAX_RATE everywhere.
❌ Mistake 2: PI = 3.0; after declaring it final.Why: final means assigned-once; the compiler rejects the betrayal.
✅ Fix: Remove final (if it must vary) or keep the single assignment.
❌ Mistake 3: Expecting final to freeze an object’s insides.Why: final locks the slip. final StringBuilder sb = ...; sb.append("x"); is perfectly legal.
✅ Fix: Want frozen content? Use String (immutable) — a later lesson.

7 Guided practice

Hints first, solutions only after a real try.

Name the magic

Replace the magic 0.18 in price * 0.18 with a named constant.

Hintfinal double TAX_RATE = 0.18;
Solutionfinal double TAX_RATE = 0.18; then price * TAX_RATE;
Spot the literal types

Name the type of each: 7, 7L, 7.0, 7.0f, ’7’, "7".

Hintint, long, double, float, char, String.
Solutionint, long, double, float, char, String — in that order.

8 Lesson quiz

3+ questions. Attempts saved locally; review queue learns your weak spots.

9 Takeaways + next step

  • Literals have default types; suffixes override them.
  • Name magic numbers as UPPER_CASE final constants.
  • Single quotes char, double quotes String.
  • final locks the reference, not the object.
🧠 Recall challengeWhich literal needs L, which needs f, and where may underscores sit?
